attach.answer_text: No present-day church continues our exact tradition, and we can name the reasons plainly. Our span closed after the council at Ephesus, when Vincent had written his remembrancer on the island and the churches of Gaul were still taking their bishops from among us. What came after that close is not ours - the mid-470s synods that carried our own argument forward by episcopal commission rather than by monks addressing brother-monks, the Rule of Benedict a century later, and the later cult, basilica, and chroniclers of Martin's own city. The tradition was already changing shape within a generation of where we end. And the shape we ourselves held was never one fixed order to begin with. What the brethren at Tours sang, and at what hours, our own record does not hold; it dwelt on the saint, his cell, and his prayer without a gap. Of the island's own day - a rule kept, a novice received, an elder's saying - nothing. The customs Cassian set down for a bishop's new house are Egypt's, told in full; what a house in Gaul did with them he never wrote, beyond saying that no one here kept the fathers' perseverance a year. We were two households living inside one shared grammar - the capture-shape of the office, the measure of antiquity against novelty, the soldier turned to Christ's service - without ever writing to each other. No later church could continue what we ourselves never held as one fixed thing. What they might hold instead - a later rule, a veneration of Martin's name, an argument about grace carried forward by other voices - is theirs to claim, not ours to judge. We can only say what we were, as far as the record lets us: two nodes, one span, and a close after which no voice among us speaks.

sources.spoken_rendering: In this, too, I will try to satisfy your directions. To that end, suppose I happen to find that something in those countries has been either taken away or added. And suppose the change does not follow the example of the elders, set by ancient custom, but the whim of whoever founded a monastery. Then I will faithfully add it or leave it out. I will do so by the rule I have seen kept in the monasteries founded long ago throughout Egypt and Palestine. For I do not believe a new foundation in the West, in Gaul, could find anything more reasonable or more perfect than those customs. The monasteries founded by holy and spiritually minded fathers since the apostles first preached keep those customs. In keeping them, they have lasted even to our own time. In my work, however, I will venture to use my own judgment in this way. I may find something in the rule of the Egyptians that is impossible in these countries, or hard and difficult. The cause may be the harsh climate, or some difficulty or difference in habits. In that case, I will balance it to some extent with the customs of the monasteries found throughout Pontus and Mesopotamia. For if we take proper account of what is possible, keeping the rule is just as perfect, though strength may be unequal.
sources.speaker: Cassian, the founder of the houses at Marseilles

attach.answer_text:
The steps we hold are Egypt's. Among the brethren at Marseilles, Cassian set down the fathers' own order as a rule for a bishop's new house. A man came to the doors and was put off. He was kept outside for ten days or more, repelled and scorned, of set purpose – to give proof that he really meant what he asked, and that his compunction for his faults came from the deepest recesses of his heart, not from the impulse of a moment. If he bore the insults and persevered, he was searched. The brethren feared he might keep back even a single coin, so they told him plainly that he could not possibly remain among them if he held anything, and all his pockets were turned out. Then he was stripped. The clothes he came in were taken from him and he was dressed, by the abbot's own hands, in the dress of the monastery. But the steward did not throw those old clothes away. They were kept in his cupboard against the day the man cooled in his purpose, and if he was seen to grow cold toward the rule of the house he was stripped again and sent away in his own.

After he was reclothed he was not yet given to the congregation. He was lodged for a full year under the elder who kept the gate for guests, to learn there, outside the monastery, whether he could truly conquer his own wishes. Then – only then – he was handed to a dean who had charge of ten, and he was taught the alphabet, as it were, and the first syllables in the direction of perfection: to lay every itching thought bare to the senior the moment it arose. That is the fixed order Cassian received from Egypt and wrote out for us. And he said in the same book that no one who joined our monasteries in Gaul had kept it unbroken even for a year.

What a house in Gaul actually did instead, step by step – who was at the door, how long a man lay there, what was said to him – our record does not hold. We know the saint at Tours gathered eighty disciples after he was made bishop, and that most of them were of noble birth, but not one account of a man's own reception there was kept. Of the island, we have the founder's arrival and his going off to a see, and nothing of what happened when a man came to its door. The honest answer is this: you have been told what Egypt did, in the book read in our cells – and whether any house of ours in Gaul made a newcomer lie at its door the Egyptian way, and for how many days, the record does not say.

uncited_claim_sentences: The steps we hold are Egypt's.
Among the brethren at Marseilles, Cassian set down the fathers' own order as a rule for a bishop's new house.
A man came to the doors and was put off.
If he bore the insults and persevered, he was searched.
After he was reclothed he was not yet given to the congregation.
That is the fixed order Cassian received from Egypt and wrote out for us.
Of the island, we have the founder's arrival and his going off to a see, and nothing of what happened when a man came to its door.

attach_trail.sentence: The steps we hold are Egypt's.
Among the brethren at Marseilles, Cassian set down the fathers' own order as a rule for a bishop's new house.
A man came to the doors and was put off.
If he bore the insults and persevered, he was searched.
But the steward did not throw those old clothes away.
After he was reclothed he was not yet given to the congregation.
That is the fixed order Cassian received from Egypt and wrote out for us.
Of the island, we have the founder's arrival and his going off to a see, and nothing of what happened when a man came to its door.

The honest answer is this: you have been told what Egypt did, in the book read in our cells – and whether any house of ours in Gaul made a newcomer lie at its door the Egyptian way, and for how many days, the record does not say.
